newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia keeps its ministers, NATO in suspense.
newsitem.headline: Russia keeps its ministers, NATO in suspense.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin continued on Thursday planning a radical government shake-up aimed at reviving Russia's flagging market reforms, while his government signalled willingness to compromise on NATO expansion.

Kremlin press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to discuss the new cabinet structure, personnel issues and financing for Russia's demoralised, cash-strapped armed forces.
It was not clear whether the meeting, following a week of high suspense and uncertainty in Russian politics, would bring any immediate announcement on the new government line-up.

"It is possible to assume that by the time the president leaves for Helsinki there will be maximum clarity in this matter," Yastrzhembsky told Ekho Moskvy radio. Yeltsin is to go to the Finnish capital on March 19 for a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Signals from Chernomydrin and the Foreign Ministry also suggested that Russia was easing longstanding opposition to NATO expansion plans, opening up the possibility of a breakthrough at the Helsinki meeting.
"We are ready to discuss constructive initiatives on the part of NATO. Recently such proposals have been appearing," Chernomyrdin told Russia's Defence Council.

Russia has for months steadfastly condemned NATO plans to invite former Eastern Bloc nations -- expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to join the alliance. But a recent flurry of diplomatic activity appears to have reduced Russian opposition.

"There has been a certain progress, although we have to say the work is hard, especially on the central question of not bringing the NATO military structure closer to the east," Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov told a briefing.
Yastrzhembsky, adding that the two presidents would also discuss U.S.-Russian economic relations, said talks in Helsinki might nonetheless be "tough".
"The (Helsinki) talks will be very concrete, rather firm and even tough because the protection of Russia's vital interests is at stake," he said.

Much as Western alliance members were waiting to see the outcome of last-minute negotiations on NATO before the Helsinki summit, dozens of Russian ministers have been kept in suspense waiting to hear of their fate.

Yeltsin, blasting the government for failing to tackle Russia's economic and social ills, last week ordered Chernomyrdin to reshuffle his team, and appointed liberal Anatoly Chubais first deputy prime minister.
Back at the helm after many months of illness, the president has made clear only Chernomyrdin and Chubais are assured of keeping their jobs.

Chubais will be the sole first deputy premier in the new line-up -- there are four now -- and the number of ministers will also be cut, helping reduce a bloated government bureaucracy little changed from Soviet times.
Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday his new cabinet, which he has promised to present by the end of the week, would be younger and more professional and include market-minded reformers.
He added that most new ministers would be under 50 and have administrative experience.

It was Yeltsin's anxiety over Russia's economic plight -- stagnant output, a big backlog in wages and pensions, low tax revenues -- which sparked his decision to draft Chubais back into the government with broad responsibility for reforms, Yastrzhembsky said.
